stances.claim: The Comelec's restriction of its checkpoint authority to a 'plain view search' — no opening of glove compartments or trunks, no body search without reasonable probable cause — is constitutionally appropriate: it correctly balances public safety necessity against the right against unreasonable searches.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-compliance affirmation: endorsing the Comelec's checkpoint design as a proper application of the plain-view exception

stances.claim: All six exceptions to the warrant requirement for searches — and both exceptions for warrantless arrests — must be construed strictly in favor of citizens and against the police officers invoking them; suspicious appearance alone (darting eyes, moving fast) can never substitute for the legal elements of each exception.
stances.rhetorical_move: strict-construction mandate: using SC precedents (Malacat, Mengote) to establish that the exceptions are narrow, not broad

notable_anecdotes: The Mengote and Malacat examples — 'darting eyes' plus 'holding one's stomach' and 'moving very fast and looking at every approaching person' — as the SC's most vivid illustrations that suspicious appearance alone, however alarming to a police officer, legally cannot justify a warrantless arrest without the specific overt-act and in-presence elements.

The Umil vs Ramos continuing-offense doctrine — a warrantless arrest valid even when the suspect is confined in a hospital, because rebellion is 'anchored on an ideological base' that never ends — presented as the counterintuitive outer boundary of the in flagrante delicto exception.

The gun-ban checkpoint as the practical trigger for a comprehensive constitutional primer — CJ uses a timely election-period policy to deliver an accessible public-education guide to arrest and search law, demonstrating his signature approach of using current events as entry points to constitutional doctrine.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses the Comelec's authorization of military/police checkpoints during the 2013 election gun ban as the entry point for a systematic constitutional guide to warrantless arrests and searches. He affirms the Comelec's restriction of its checkpoints to 'plain view search' -- visual inspection only, no opening of glove compartments or trunks, no body search without reasonable probable cause -- as constitutionally sound. He then surveys the three exceptions to the warrant requirement for arrests: in flagrante delicto (overt act + in presence of arresting officer; suspicious appearance alone -- 'darting eyes,' 'moving very fast' -- is insufficient per Mengote and Malacat); hot pursuit (prior committed offense + arresting officer's personal knowledge, not mere intelligence information); and the continuing-offense doctrine (Umil vs Ramos -- rebellion is 'anchored on an ideological base,' so a warrantless arrest is valid even when the suspect is hospitalized). For warrantless searches, he catalogues six exceptions: (1) incident to lawful arrest; (2) plain view; (3) vehicle searches (allowed more liberally for public safety); (4) customs searches; (5) consented searches; (6) stop and frisk. He closes with the governing meta-rule: the general rule is 'no warrant, no arrest, no search,' and all exceptions -- including Comelec checkpoints -- must be construed strictly in favor of the people.
